newsitem.title: SPAIN: Latin America needs more reforms for secure growth.
newsitem.headline: Latin America needs more reforms for secure growth.

text.p: Despite 10 years of reforms, Latin America must press ahead with liberalisation measures many citizens distrust if it is to secure sustainable growth, the Inter-American Development Bank said on Sunday.

Fewer restrictions on capital movement and investment have lowered inflation, stabilised currencies, boosted growth and income levels across the region, but poverty remains high and wealth inequitably distributed, according to an IADB study.

"The reforms have accelerated growth and lowered volatility but the achievements are not sufficient and growth is not what was expected," said IADB chief economist Ricardo Hausmann, presenting a study evaluating 10 years of Latin American reform.
Latin America has embarked over the past decade on a far-reaching reform programme designed to reduce inflation, slash deficits and open its economies to foreign investors.
Latin Americans remain largely dissastisfied with their lot and unconvinced that further liberalisation will improve it, according to an IADB survey.
In an opinion poll, 75 percent of those surveyed said they believed poverty had risen during the last 10 years, while 61 percent saw no improvement.

And, despite 10 years of reforms, a liberal economic model of private enterprise won no more popular support in the poll than a mixed model of state and private ownership, or one in which workers would have a larger voice.
Brazilian Minister of Planning Antonio Kandir said the reforms' poor reception stemmed not from their inefficiency but from disappointed hopes for even greater improvement.

"Reforms done in an inadequate fashion, promising more than can be delivered, hurt the credibility of the government... and end up hurting the efficiency of the reforms," Kandir told a seminar before the IADB's annual meeting begins on Monday.

The IADB report urged more in-depth change, saying that without the reforms undertaken during the last 10 years, per capita income in Latin America would now be 20 percent lower at $2,400 a year instead of the current $3,000.
The distribution of income in Latin America remained the most unequal in the world, although the concentration of wealth has not increased over this period, the study showed.
"The reforms have helped, but more needs to be done to ensure the macroeconomic stability required for accelerated and more equitable long-run growth in the region," the study said.
The regional growth rate could climb to eight percent in a decade -- on a par with the so-called tiger economies of Southeast Asia -- with tax and labour reform, privatisations and better education.
The Asian and Latin American labour force were neck and neck in terms of education two decades ago, but Asians now have on average nine years of education while Latin Americans have just five.
But other experts warned that there might be little tolerance left among the public for such economic reforms.

"If they can't show consistent growth over time the populations may start rejecting some of these reforms," said William Rhodes, now vice chairman of Citibank and a leading debt negotiator for Latin America during the 1980s debt crisis.
